title: The Prophets close
hook: the Talmud says after the prophets, prophecy passed to the wise, and to children and fools (Bava Batra 12b)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Malachi's promise: hearts turned between parents and children. Your line was turn the hearts. Today, the prophets go quiet.

Malachi rolls up, and the section of the Bible called the Prophets is done. This year opened it the day Moses died, with Joshua told to be strong. Since then: judges and kings, prophets who argued, wept and waited, and the Twelve, from Hosea's broken marriage to Malachi's turning hearts. And then silence. The rabbis felt that silence, and they asked: when the prophets stop, where does the voice go? Their answer, in the Talmud's tractate Bava Batra, has a surprise at the end.
screen: `MALACHI ROLLS UP.` → `JOSHUA TO MALACHI.` → `WHERE DOES THE VOICE GO?`

segments.voice: Here is the passage, retold. Rabbi Avdimi of Haifa teaches: from the day the Temple was destroyed, prophecy was taken from the prophets and given to the wise. The Talmud pushes back: isn't a sage a prophet too? It answers that prophecy was taken from the prophets, but not from the wise. Then a teacher named Amemar adds: the sage is greater than the prophet. A bold thing to say, and it tells you how the rabbis saw their own work. The voice didn't vanish. It moved into study: into people sitting with these very books, arguing over a verse, asking what it asks of us now. Every one of these days, from Micah's three verbs to Habakkuk's one line, has been that kind of listening. Then the surprise. Rabbi Yochanan says: from the day the Temple was destroyed, prophecy was taken from the prophets and given to fools and to children. The Talmud even tells of a passing remark, from someone nobody took seriously, that turned out to be true. Readers hear this in more than one way. Some hear a joke with an edge: prophecy is so cheapened that only fools speak it. Others hear something tender: the truth now turns up where nobody guards it. A child says the thing every adult in the room was too careful to say. A stranger's offhand line answers the question you've carried for a month. Both readings agree on this much. The scrolls are finished. The listening isn't.
screen: `GIVEN TO THE WISE.` · `THE SAGE IS GREATER THAN THE PROPHET.` · then, large: `GIVEN TO FOOLS AND TO CHILDREN.` · then: `THE PROPHETS CLOSE, LISTENING DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something a child once said that stopped you, a question you couldn't answer, a blunt truth at the dinner table, a small kindness they didn't know was big; if no child comes to mind, think of someone you don't usually listen to, and something they said that turned out right. Hold their words, then simply listen to the room around you, the small sounds nobody guards. If you pray, you can let the listening be your prayer.
Bava Batra, the Talmud tractate where the rabbis say that when the Prophets closed, their voice passed to the wise, and to fools and children. Today's word.
Your line: the voice goes on. Given to the wise, and to fools and children. Day eight hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Jews read from the Prophets in synagogue on Shabbat and festivals as the haftarah, and the Talmud's discussion of where prophecy went is studied as part of the tradition's own account of rabbinic learning.

chat.says: When the prophets stopped, did God's voice just disappear?
options: The rabbis said prophecy passed to the wise, and even to fools and children.
The rabbis said it disappeared, and no one has heard a true word since.
The rabbis said it passed to the kings, who spoke for God from then on.
